title: A way out
hook: whoever is mindful of Allah, He makes a way out and provides from where he never expects (65:2–3)

segments.voice: Yesterday: ma'ruf, from the surah named divorce. Your line was part with kindness.

Some problems have walls on every side. The rent and the paycheck don't meet. The diagnosis has no good option. The family fight has gone on so long nobody remembers how it started. The math gets run again at two in the morning, and every road ends in the same brick. In exactly that spot, some Muslims reach for one line from the Qur'an. It isn't in a chapter about miracles or battles. It sits in the middle of yesterday's surah, between the rules for divorce.

Surah at-Talaq, verses two and three. Pickthall: "And whosoever keepeth his duty to Allah, Allah will appoint a way out for him, And will provide for him from (a quarter) whence he hath no expectation." Keeping your duty is Pickthall's phrase for taqwa: mindfulness of Allah, living as someone who knows they're seen. The way out is one Arabic word, makhraj, from the root for going out. Not a cure for every problem. An exit. The second promise is stranger: provision from where you never expected. Not from the road you were staring at. From somewhere off the map. Then: whoever puts their trust in Allah, He is enough for them. Now notice where this sits. The verses around it are about the waiting period, the house, the witnesses, the money owed when a marriage ends. Some commentators read the placement as deliberate. Divorce is a place where people can feel trapped: by money, by children, by fear of being alone. And right there, in the middle of the rules, the Qur'an breaks in with hope. It doesn't promise the exit you wanted. It doesn't say when. It says the walls are not the whole story. Some Muslims memorize these two verses and repeat them when a problem has no visible door, not as a trick to make it vanish, but as a way to keep doing the right thing while they wait for the door they can't see yet.
screen: `TAQWA: LIVING AS ONE WHO IS SEEN.`
`HOPE IN THE MIDDLE OF THE RULES.`

segments.voice: Let one real problem come to mind, the one with walls, and name it silently in one sentence without trying to solve it. Picture it as a room where you've been staring at the same wall, and let your attention drift to the corners you haven't looked at. If you pray, hold the verse there: a way out, from where you never expected; if not, just breathe with the problem without pushing on it.
Makhraj, an exit, promised in 65:2 to whoever keeps their duty to Allah, with provision from where they never expected. Today's word.
Your line: a way out comes. Sometimes from a corner you weren't watching. Six hundred thirty-three days in.

howItsDone: Some Muslims memorize 65:2–3 and recite it in times of debt, illness or family trouble, alongside the promise that whoever trusts in Allah, He is enough for them.
